How does Alaska ranked-choice voting work? Rules and 2026 Senate use. Alaska ranked-choice voting is a system in which voters rank candidates in order of preference, and counting continues in rounds until one candidate holds a majority. Under this system, a voter's lower choice can count if a first choice is eliminated, which can delay the final result in close contests.. Alaska's Senate race between Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola is among the close contests in the 2026 midterms, and it is being counted under the state's ranked-choice system. Results there were still pending on election night.. Sources in this set confirm that the system shapes the 2026 U.S. Senate race in Alaska, where Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola. BBC reporting describes Alaska's ranked-choice system as adding uncertainty to the contest, and notes that the state is one of the slower ones to reach an outcome. The NBC News results page listed the Alaska Senate race as too early to call on the night of the vote, with Peltola at 48.2 percent and Sullivan at 47.9 percent, and 75.5 percent of the vote counted. The same page showed the state's count was still in progress while other races had been decided.
